Opening

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Turn Earth, Explain the Sky · Classic

Learning objective

I can use Earth’s rotation to explain day, night and the Sun’s apparent daily movement.

Success looks like

  • Locate a place on the lit or unlit side.
  • Order a day–night cycle using the fixed-light model.
  • Explain an observation and one model limit.

A separate 40-minute Classic alternative. Use this Q-card mission instead of the Day and Night pair when a single-session explanation is appropriate.

One 40-minute Classic alternative

Use this self-contained lesson instead of the paired version where appropriate. It is not an extra compulsory week.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Choose one route; equivalent science evidence does not require a written conversion.

Four clues to start

Supported · 4 questions

1. Observer

At RIGHT, does the observer face towards or away from a Sun fixed LEFT?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Follow the light direction.

2. Motion

What must turn in this daily-cycle model?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Keep the lamp fixed.

Answer guidance

Answer: The Earth model.

3. Day length

A solar day is about 24 hours or 365 days?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. A day is not a year.

Answer guidance

Answer: About 24 hours.

4. Evidence

Is “the marker is unlit” an observation or a claim that the Sun went out?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Describe only what you can see.

Answer: An observation.

I do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · LESSON A · 7 MINUTES

Watch, predict, explain

Predict, model, explain

The place moves into or out of sunlight because Earth turns; the Sun does not switch off.

Make a prediction. Change one view, then use a label to explain what you notice.

At TOP the observer enters light. Classic Q-D is sunrise; these labels differ from the paired pack.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Classic Q labels: A = LEFT/noon, B = BOTTOM/sunset, C = RIGHT/night, D = TOP/sunrise. Cycle A → B → C → D → A. Do not interchange with the paired lesson’s C/D/B/A labels. Sun fixed LEFT; above-North-Pole view turns anticlockwise. This ideal equatorial model is not a scale model or an exact sunrise-time prediction.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Q-D · Sunrise
At TOP the observer enters light. Classic Q-D is sunrise; these labels differ from the paired pack.

08–16 seconds · Q-A · Noon
At LEFT the observer faces the fixed source. Classic Q-A is model noon.

16–24 seconds · Q-B · Sunset
At BOTTOM the observer leaves the lit half. Classic Q-B is sunset.

24–32 seconds · Q-C · Night
At RIGHT the observer faces away from the light. Classic Q-C is night.

Fits the model

Needs a correction

Choose a card first. No cards have been placed.

Read the card clues

Q-A noon: LEFT faces the fixed light.

Q-B sunset: BOTTOM leaves light as the marker turns anticlockwise.

Q-C night: RIGHT faces away from the source.

Q-D sunrise: TOP enters the lit half.

The lamp circles Earth each day: The daily-cycle model keeps the source fixed and rotates Earth.

Exact time from a drawing: The model does not include all conditions needed for exact local sunrise times.

You do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · LESSON A · 10 MINUTES

Use the evidence yourself

Supported · use one response mode

1. Place Q cards

Match Q-A noon, Q-B sunset, Q-C night and Q-D sunrise to positions.

Help: Sun LEFT; TOP enters light.

2. Explain a transition

Explain Q-B sunset to Q-C night with “turns away”.

Help: The lamp remains on.

3. Limit the claim

Choose “not to scale” as one model limit.

Help: A small drawing is not the real Earth.

Standard · use one response mode

1. Place Q cards

Place all four Q cards and draw the rotation arrow.

Help: A → B → C → D.

2. Explain a transition

Use two Q positions to explain a changing sky report.

Help: Compare lit and unlit sides.

3. Limit the claim

State why the model cannot give an exact sunrise time.

Help: Latitude, date and tilt matter.

Stretch · use one response mode

1. Place Q cards

Justify all four placements using a consistent north-pole view.

Help: Turn anticlockwise.

2. Explain a transition

Explain how an observer’s rotation causes apparent Sun movement.

Help: Actual apparent motion is an observation.

3. Limit the claim

Explain why a solar day differs from a full orbit and name a model limit.

Help: About 24 hours versus about one year.

Use the application model · an alternative to writing

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Exit

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Q-card cycle

After Q-A noon, choose Q-B sunset or Q-D sunrise.

Help beside the question
Continue anticlockwise.

Answer guidance

Answer: Q-B sunset.

2. Sky explanation

Explain the Sun’s apparent daily motion using Earth’s rotation.

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Earth turns west to east.

Answer guidance

Answer: As Earth rotates west to east, the Sun appears to move generally east to west across the observer’s sky.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Q-card cycle

Starting at Q-A noon, order the next Classic cards.

Help beside the question
A LEFT → B BOTTOM → C RIGHT → D TOP.

Answer guidance

Answer: A → B → C → D → A.

2. Sky explanation

Explain the Sun’s apparent daily motion using Earth’s rotation.

Help beside the question
Earth turns west to east.

Answer guidance

Answer: As Earth rotates west to east, the Sun appears to move generally east to west across the observer’s sky.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Q-card cycle

Starting at Q-A noon, order the next Classic cards.

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. A LEFT → B BOTTOM → C RIGHT → D TOP.

Answer guidance

Answer: A → B → C → D → A.

2. Sky explanation

Give the rotation explanation and one limit of the model.

Help beside the question
Do not state exact sunrise times.

Answer guidance

Answer: Earth’s west-to-east rotation changes the observer’s view; the simplified model omits latitude, tilt and season.

Knowledge organiser

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can use Earth’s rotation to explain day, night and the Sun’s apparent daily movement.

Key words

rotation — a turn around an axis

axis — imaginary line through Earth’s poles

daylight — the Sun is above the local horizon

apparent movement — movement seen by an observer

orbit — a path around another body

Remember

  • Earth rotates west to east.
  • About 24 hours is one solar day.
  • The side facing the Sun is lit; the far side is dark.
  • The Sun appears to cross the sky mainly because Earth rotates.

Success looks like

  • Locate a place on the lit or unlit side.
  • Order a day–night cycle using the fixed-light model.
  • Explain an observation and one model limit.

The place moves into or out of sunlight because Earth turns; the Sun does not switch off.

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Use a cool LED lamp and a large ball, or the supplied diagrams. Secure cables; keep safe room lighting. Never look at the Sun. An adult may turn the model while the pupil directs.

Scientific care

Classic Q labels: A = LEFT/noon, B = BOTTOM/sunset, C = RIGHT/night, D = TOP/sunrise. Cycle A → B → C → D → A. Do not interchange with the paired lesson’s C/D/B/A labels. Sun fixed LEFT; above-North-Pole view turns anticlockwise. This ideal equatorial model is not a scale model or an exact sunrise-time prediction.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Sources and scope

  • NASA · Earth and day/night
  • NASA · Reference systems: solar and sidereal days
  • Original lesson A

Staff · feedback and access

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Audience and response

The lesson teacher is the named adult audience. Hear or read the pupil’s own science response. A click, downloaded file or completed box is not evidence that a request was heard.

Respond within the existing task

Offer reading help, fewer cards at once, clearer labels, an adult-directed model or additional thinking time. Say what can and cannot change, then check whether the adjustment helped.

No additional pupil artefact

A response can be spoken, pointed, signed, drawn or written. Do not require a separate Lundy record, signature or written conversion of an oral response.

An optional pupil-owned note such as “What I said, and what it changed” may be used in existing work. It is not a requirement. If scribing, keep the pupil’s own words; the adult is an audience, not a verifier.

Keep assessment honest

Use current school recording practice and unit criteria separately. This pack does not certify an award. Do not infer a policy code from automated checking or a download.
